progression.startsWith: Around 1900, many Australians died of diseases they caught from someone else, like pneumonia and tuberculosis. Today, most Australians die of diseases nobody can catch: heart disease, dementia, stroke and lung cancer. That's partly because vaccines, antibiotics and clean water now prevent many deaths from infection, so more people live long enough for these slower diseases to develop. So if a disease isn't caught, what causes it?
progression.stopsAfter: stating that an infectious disease is caused by a pathogen invading and multiplying in the body (many, not all, pass between hosts), and a non-infectious disease is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be caught, so the dividing line is the cause, not severity or genes (cystic fibrosis is genetic and non-infectious); naming the four groups of cause with a plain meaning each (genetic: a DNA change alters a protein; environmental: an outside exposure damages cells; nutritional: too little or too much of a nutrient; cancer: cells dividing out of control, whatever the trigger); tracing cystic fibrosis from two altered CFTR genes to a misfolded channel that is broken down before it reaches the membrane, to less chloride and water leaving the airway cells, to thick mucus that cilia cannot clear, to repeated lung infections, with thick mucus as the effect, not the cause; explaining silicosis (inhaled silica dust, immune cells cannot break it down, scarring, stiff lungs), iron-deficiency anaemia (too little iron taken in or absorbed, less haemoglobin, smaller paler red cells, less oxygen carried) and melanoma (UV-triggered damage to genes that control division, a cancer with an environmental trigger); saying most diseases are multifactorial and classifying by the main contributing factor with its mechanism; classifying three unseen conditions and resolving an infectious trigger; tracing an unseen genetic disease (FH) from gene to body.
progression.nextLesson: how environmental exposure causes disease (bio-m8-b07), then nutrition (b08) and cancer (b09).

teaching.task: Most Australians now die of diseases nobody can catch. If a disease isn't caught, what causes it?
teaching.causalExplanation: Start with the dividing line. An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen, like a bacterium or virus, invading and multiplying in the body. Many, but not all, can pass between hosts. A non-infectious disease isn't caused by a pathogen, so you can't catch it. The test is the cause. It isn't about how serious the disease is, or whether genes are involved. Cystic fibrosis is genetic, and it's still non-infectious, because no pathogen causes it. So what does cause them? The causes fall into four groups. A genetic disease starts with a change in DNA that alters a protein. An environmental disease starts with something from outside the body that damages cells. A nutritional disease comes from too little, or too much, of a nutrient. And cancer is cells dividing out of control. For each one, trace the same chain: the cause, what changes in the cells, and the effect on the body. Start with a genetic disease, cystic fibrosis. Cells lining your airways make a protein called CFTR, from the CFTR gene. It's a channel in the cell membrane that lets chloride ions out onto the airway surface. Water follows the chloride by osmosis, so the mucus there stays thin and runny, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it, with any trapped bacteria, up and out.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Around 1900, many Australians died of diseases they caught from someone else, like pneumonia and tuberculosis. Start with the dividing line. So what does cause them? The causes fall into four groups. Start with a genetic disease, cystic fibrosis. In cystic fibrosis, both copies of the CFTR gene are altered. Notice the order. An environmental disease starts outside the body. Too little available iron, from a poor diet or poor absorption, can cause a nutritional deficiency disease. Cancer gets its own group, because it's defined by what the cells do, not by what started it. Real diseases often have several causes acting together. Two exam questions. Goitre is nutritional: too little iodine, so the thyroid can't make enough hormone and enlarges. Second. The altered gene means fewer working LDL receptors on liver cells. So for any disease, first ask: is it caused by a pathogen? If not, ask what kind of disease it is: genetic, environmental, nutritional, or cancer.

teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. Three conditions are described on screen: goitre, Huntington's disease and cervical cancer. Classify each one into a group. Then explain why a student who says cervical cancer is infectious is wrong. Pause here to answer. Second. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is caused by an altered LDLR gene. Normally, this gene codes for a receptor on liver cells that removes LDL cholesterol from the blood. Explain how the altered gene can lead to heart disease. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: Scope: the opening video of the Module 8 Causes and Effects block (B8-IQ2-01). Route entry **bio-m8-b06** ("What causes a non-infectious disease?", type core, site lessons L06 and L07, syllabus action B8-IQ2-01, prerequisites bio-m6-b05 and bio-m7-b01, playlist order 8, plan anchor B06, next bio-m8-b07), from `../../module8-video-route-draft.json`. Route start: "Separate inherited and acquired causes from infection." Route stop: "Trace a genetic variant through protein and body effect." **Entry knowledge:** bio-m7-b01 (an infectious disease is caused by a pathogen, and most can pass between hosts; tuberculosis against type 2 diabetes); bio-m6-b05 (somatic mutations in body cells can start a cancer; germ-line mutations can be inherited); from Module 5, bio-m5-b07 (one base change traced through haemoglobin's shape to sickle cells and the trait) and bio-m5-b09 (autosomal recessive conditions such as cystic fibrosis need two altered alleles; carriers). Year 11: osmosis, cell membranes. **Start:** the dividing line between infectious and non-infectious disease (whether a pathogen causes it, not transmission alone, severity or genes). **Stop:** classify a cause into one of the four syllabus groups with one example each, and trace one genetic disease, cystic fibrosis, from gene to protein to cells to body. **Next handoff:** bio-m8-b07, "How does environmental exposure cause disease?" (then b08 nutrition and b09 cancer, which carry the detail this video leaves out). Visual: a four-column board writes, one column per cue, each with a one-line meaning and a small thumbnail: "genetic: a DNA change alters a protein" (`m5x-cell-protein-synthesis-v1.png`), "environmental: an outside exposure damages cells" (new `m8-lungs-silicosis-v1.png`, small), "nutritional: too little or too much of a nutrient" (`m5x-red-blood-cells-v1.png`), "cancer: cells dividing out of control" (`b5x-cell-dividing-v1.png`). Each column dims to its header as the next lights. On "chain" the board shrinks to the `GroupTab` at the upper left (four chips) and the `CauseChain` strip draws along the bottom: "cause" → "what changes in the cells" → "effect on the body" (empty slots). Grey tag under the strip: "the syllabus lists these four". At most three bright items. Hold one second. - Confirm the dotpoint wording against `docs/production/programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json` and the YouTube title length (100 characters or fewer). Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 8): - Dotpoint wording confirmed against `docs/production/programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json` (B8-IQ2-01 and its four listed examples, p 57). - **Term load.** New spoken terms: non-infectious, genetic, environmental, nutritional, cancer (as groups), CFTR, chloride, cilia, carriers (recalled), silicosis, haemoglobin, anaemia, tumour, melanoma, multifactorial. That is heavier than b05; the four group names are syllabus words students will read anyway, and each example term arrives after its mechanism. The learning review should check scenes 4 and 5 at playback speed (CFTR, chloride, osmosis and cilia arrive together in scene 4).

scenes.visualReference: the group tab lights "cancer". Centre: m8-skin-normal-v1.png large. scenes.teachingReason: Cancer gets its own group, because it's defined by what the cells do, not by what started it.

scenes.visualReference: the board clears; the chain strip and tab dim to grey. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "Condition 1, goitre: the thyroid gland enlarges when the diet contains too little iodine, which the thyroid needs to make the hormone thyroxine. Condition 2, Huntington's disease: one altered copy of the HTT gene leads to a harmful protein that damages brain cells. Condition 3, cervical cancer: cells of the cervix divide out of control after a long-lasting human papillomavirus (HPV) infection." Demand: "(a) Classify each condition as genetic, environmental, nutritional or cancer. (2 marks) (b) A student says cervical cancer is an infectious disease because a virus is involved. Explain why the student is incorrect. (2 marks)". No plates. The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.
